summary: Comments from UCLA-CCN on the proposed Data Transfer Protocol and File Transfer Protocol. They say separators in one DTP mode need sequence numbers, the modes-available handshake should not be mandatory, and in FTP ending a file by closing the connection should signal an error, not a normal end.

eli5.summary: Someone reads the draft rules for sending files and says what to fix. For example, a file should end with a clear signal, not by hanging up the phone.

subtitle: Feedback on early draft file transfer and data transfer protocols.

tldr.problem: Early drafts of the Data Transfer Protocol and File Transfer Protocol have design issues that could cause problems in practice.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 238 from UCLA-CCN provides detailed comments on specific problems in both protocols, including missing sequence numbers, unnecessary handshakes, and incorrect error signaling.
tldr.outcome: The feedback led to corrections in later protocol versions, and is cited as an example of the design review process for early internet protocols.

today: RFC 238 is not Internet Standard but is an important historical document. It shows how protocol flaws were identified and fixed in the early network. The principle that connection closure should signal clear state (success vs. error) became standard in later internet protocols.

sections.title: Protocol Feedback
sections.content:
R. T. Braden at UCLA's CCN (Communications Control Network) analyzed draft proposals for the Data Transfer Protocol (DTP) and File Transfer Protocol (FTP) and found several design problems. This RFC updates RFC 171 and RFC 172 with detailed comments on what needs to change.

Braden's feedback reflects the collaborative design process of early network protocols, where multiple sites reviewed drafts and raised issues before final adoption.
sections.eli5: Someone read the draft rules and found problems that could cause data loss or confusion.

sections.title: Data Transfer Protocol Issues
sections.content:
In the Descriptor/Count mode of DTP, Information Separators should include a transaction sequence number field. Without sequence numbers, a receiver cannot be sure all transactions arrived before a separation marker. This requires two forms of separators: one for Descriptor/Count mode and one for DLE (Data Link Escape) mode.

The second issue is that the modes-available handshake should not be mandatory. In simplex (one-way) transmission, the receiver only cares what mode the transmitter actually uses, discovered when the first data arrives. Even in duplex (two-way) mode, the initial handshake wastes time and protocol complexity.
sections.eli5: Separators need numbers so you know no chunks got lost. And both sides do not need to shake hands about which mode to use before sending data.

sections.title: File Transfer Protocol Issues
sections.content:
FTP's most serious problem is allowing an end-of-file to be indicated by closing the connection. Braden notes this is the same mistake made in an early NETRJS implementation. Closing without a File Separator transaction should only signal an error or abort, never normal completion. The receiver has no way to distinguish between a normal close and a host crash.

Braden also recommends two forms of the store request: one that fails if a file exists, one that replaces it. Service hosts should be allowed to demand username and password transactions. Error codes should permit explanatory text, and error transactions should handle lost data and lost synchronization.
sections.eli5: Hanging up the phone should mean error, not done. Let the server require passwords. Add numbers to errors so people can explain what went wrong.

sections.title: Design Review
sections.content:
RFC 238 exemplifies the collaborative design process that shaped early internet protocols. Rather than one site imposing a design, the RFC process allowed multiple implementations and sites to review proposals and raise issues.

Braden's specific, practical concerns were based on real implementation experience. The emphasis on signal clarity (close means error, not success) and the inclusion of explanatory text in errors show thinking about operational reliability that would become standard practice.
sections.eli5: This is how protocol design worked: one site made a draft, others read it and said what was wrong, then the authors fixed it.
